chapterTitle: Understanding Redis Data Persistence and Configuration

screens.title: Understanding Redis Data Persistence and Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Redis is a memory-first database, which makes it very fast, but also means data in memory will be lost unless you persist it. In this lesson you will learn the two primary persistence mechanisms Redis provides: RDB snapshots, which capture point-in-time binary images of your dataset, and AOF logging, which records a journal of every write operation. You will see the tradeoffs: RDB is compact and excellent for fast restarts and backups but can lose recent writes between snapshots; AOF provides stronger durability by replaying commands but can grow larger and slow restarts. You will also learn the key redis. conf directives that control persistence, how to run manual saves safely using SAVE and BGSAVE, and practical scenarios where RDB only, AOF only, or a combined approach is appropriate. By the end, you will be able to choose a configuration that balances durability, performance, and operational safety for your application.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Understanding Redis Data Persistence
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Understanding Redis Data Persistence

Why in-memory speed and on-disk durability must be balanced, and how Redis gives two complementary persistence options.

Duration: 15–25 minutes
In this lesson
  • How RDB snapshots work and when to use them.
  • How AOF logging records every write and how to configure fsync.
  • Practical configuration and manual save commands.
Coming up

Guided configuration choices and safety practices for persistence directories and file rewrites.

Explore Key Topics
RDB Snapshots
Point-in-time binary backups for fast restarts and compact files.
AOF Logging
Append-only journal of write commands for better durability.
Configuration
redis.conf directives like save, appendonly, appendfsync, and dir.
Visual Concept
RDB: snapshot file
AOF: append-only log
Combined: backup + durability
Why this matters

Your choice of persistence affects how much recent data you might lose, how fast Redis restarts, and how large on-disk files grow. This lesson helps you match choices to application needs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build practical skills with Redis persistence. First, you will be able to distinguish RDB and AOF, explaining how each mechanism stores data and how they affect restart time and recovery guarantees. Second, you will learn how RDB snapshots are created and why Redis forks a child process to write the file, which keeps the server responsive during backups. Third, you will learn how AOF logs every write as a sequence of commands and how fsync choices control durability and performance. Finally, you will practice changing redis. conf settings and running manual commands like SAVE, BGSAVE, and BGREWRITEAOF. Each objective includes a small hands-on mental model so you can predict behavior during a crash and choose the right configuration for your application's tolerance for data loss. These skills will help you operate Redis with confidence and avoid common mistakes like running out of disk space during a save.

screens.title: Why persistence matters for an in-memory database
screens.narratorSegment: Persistence is the ability of Redis to store its in-memory dataset on disk so data survives restarts or crashes. Because Redis primarily serves and manipulates data in memory for speed, volatility is an inherent risk: if the process crashes or the host reboots, all volatile state disappears unless persisted. Practically, persistence turns an in-memory snapshot into a recoverable on-disk artifact. One concrete example: a session store using Redis without persistence could lose all active sessions after a restart, forcing users to reauthenticate. A common misconception is that persistence is only for databases that are not caches. In reality, many caching deployments also need persistence for warm restarts or graceful failover. Another misconception is that persistence eliminates every risk; it does not. Different persistence mechanisms trade off potential data loss windows, restart performance, and file size. The core decision is about acceptable data-loss tolerance. If your application can accept some recent writes being lost, RDB snapshots might be enough. If you require near-zero data loss, AOF with frequent fsync is preferable. Reflect: what data in your application cannot be recreated, and how much recent data loss would be tolerable?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Persistence prevents total data loss after crashes by writing Redis state or write history to disk; the mechanism chosen controls durability and restart behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Why persistence matters
Core Concept

What persistence means for Redis

Persistence converts volatile memory state into on-disk artifacts so data survives process or host failures.

  • Persistence protects against full data loss after crashes or restarts.
  • Different mechanisms give different recovery guarantees and performance tradeoffs.
  • Decide based on how much recent write loss your application can tolerate.
Concrete example
A session cache without persistence loses all sessions on restart, requiring reauthentication for users.
Common mistake
Assuming persistence means zero risk. In fact, the mechanism defines how much recent data can be lost.
Key Takeaway

Think in terms of acceptable data-loss windows and how persistence choices change restart and recovery behavior.

Annotated concept
Volatile memory: fast but temporary
Persistence: durability via RDB or AOF
Operational impact: restart time and file size tradeoffs
Reflection
List the data types in your app that cannot be reconstructed and decide whether occasional loss is acceptable for them.

screens.title: How RDB snapshots work
screens.narratorSegment: RDB persistence creates point-in-time snapshots of the Redis dataset. The process begins when Redis decides to snapshot—either automatically via save directives or manually via SAVE/BGSAVE. Redis forks a child process; the child writes the entire dataset to a temporary RDB file on disk while the parent continues serving clients. When the child finishes writing and the file is safely on disk, Redis atomically replaces the old RDB with the new file. This fork-and-write approach offloads disk input and output to the child and keeps the main process responsive. A concrete example: a configuration like save 900 1 will create a snapshot if at least one write happens within 900 seconds. The main misconception to avoid is thinking RDB writes every change; it does not. It captures periodic full images, so any writes after the last snapshot but before a crash are lost. Advantages are compact binary files and fast restarts, making RDB excellent for backups and disaster recovery. Disadvantages are the data-loss window and the need for disk space to hold both temporary and final RDB files during writes. How RDB snapshots work means rdb uses a forked child to write a full binary snapshot to a temporary file then replaces the previous snapshot, balancing responsiveness and compact backups.. In practical terms, fork, write temporary file, and replace for compact backups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › RDB Snapshots
Process Flow

Fork → Child writes RDB → Replace

RDB takes full point-in-time snapshots using a child process to perform disk I/O so Redis stays responsive.

  1. Trigger: automatic save directive or manual BGSAVE/SAVE.
  2. Fork: Redis creates a child process to write the snapshot.
  3. Write: child writes to a temporary RDB file.
  4. Replace: on success, the temporary file atomically replaces the old RDB.
Advantage
Compact binary files and fast restarts; ideal for backups.
Disadvantage
Possible loss of writes between snapshots; requires disk space for temporary file.
Example
If redis.conf contains save 900 1, Redis will snapshot if one or more writes occur within 900 seconds. This creates a full binary file representing the dataset at that moment.
Common mistake
Assuming snapshots are continuous. RDB snapshots capture discrete moments only; they are not a command journal.
Key Takeaway

Use RDB for compact backups and fast restarts when some recent write loss is acceptable.

screens.title: What is AOF (Append Only File) logging
screens.narratorSegment: AOF persistence records every write command Redis receives into an append-only log. Instead of saving full snapshots, AOF writes a sequence of redis commands that can be replayed at restart to reconstruct the dataset. This approach is like keeping a journal of changes: when Redis restarts it replays the logged commands in order to restore state. A key configuration is appendfsync, which controls when Redis calls fsync to flush buffered writes to physical disk. The common settings are always, everysec, and no. Using everysec is a practical compromise: it flushes the AOF roughly once per second, limiting potential data loss to about one second while keeping write latency low. A concrete example: enabling appendonly yes and appendfsync everysec causes every write to be appended immediately and the OS to be asked to flush the log at most once per second. Misconceptions include thinking AOF is always faster or smaller than RDB; in fact AOF files can be larger and restarts slower because commands must be replayed. AOF plus periodic rewrites gives strong durability with manageable file size growth. What is AOF (Append Only File) logging means aof logs all write commands for replay-based recovery; appendfsync controls durability versus performance tradeoffs.. In practical terms, a write-journal approach that records every write operation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › AOF Logging
Definition

Append-only log of write commands

AOF writes each write command to a log that can be replayed to rebuild the dataset on restart.

  • AOF records a sequence of write commands rather than full snapshots.
  • On restart, Redis re-executes the recorded commands to restore state.
  • appendfsync controls how frequently the log is flushed to disk.
Durability
Better durability than RDB when fsync is frequent.
Tradeoffs
Larger files and slower restarts due to command replay.
Configuration example
# Enable AOF and choose fsync policy
appendonly yes
appendfilename "appendonly.aof"
appendfsync everysec
Common misconception
Assuming appendonly always gives zero data loss. In practice, fsync policy determines the actual durability window.
Key Takeaway

Use AOF when you need tighter durability and configure appendfsync according to your latency tolerance.

screens.title: AOF growth and rewrite: BGREWRITEAOF
screens.narratorSegment: As writes accumulate, the append-only file grows because it stores every modifying command. To prevent unbounded growth and to remove redundant commands, Redis supports an automatic rewrite mechanism and the manual BGREWRITEAOF command. When rewriting, Redis creates a new optimized AOF by reading the current dataset and emitting a minimal set of commands that recreate it. This reduces file size and speeds up restarts. The auto-aof-rewrite-percentage and auto-aof-rewrite-min-size settings control when Redis triggers the rewrite; for example auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100 means a rewrite runs when the AOF grows by 100% since the last rewrite. A common misunderstanding is that rewrites block the server. BGREWRITEAOF is asynchronous: it forks a child to create the new file, allowing the parent to continue serving clients. However, rewriting requires disk space for the temporary file and imposes extra input and output, so you must ensure sufficient disk capacity and monitor load. If a rewrite is interrupted or the disk fills, the AOF may remain large or become inconsistent, so keep backups and monitor rewrite activity. AOF growth and rewrite: BGREWRITEAOF means bgrewriteaof creates a compact aof by rewriting commands from the current dataset; it runs asynchronously but needs disk space and i/o monitoring.. In practical terms, how aof can be compacted and the rewrite trigger. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AOF rewrite
keyIdea.text: BGREWRITEAOF creates a compact AOF by rewriting commands from the current dataset; it runs asynchronously but needs disk space and I/O monitoring.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › AOF Rewrites
Process

BGREWRITEAOF: compacting the AOF

Rewriting reads the dataset and emits a minimal command sequence to recreate it, removing redundant writes.

Rewrite triggers: auto-aof-rewrite-percentage and min-size settings. Example: percentage 100 triggers when AOF doubles.
Rewrite runs asynchronously by forking a child; the parent continues serving requests.
Requires disk space for temporary file and additional I/O during rewrite.
Common mistake
Not reserving disk space for the temporary rewritten AOF, which can cause rewrite failure and data risk.
Config snippet
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb
Concrete example
If your AOF was 50 megabytes, with percentage 100 a rewrite will be triggered when it grows to 100 megabytes since the last rewrite.
Key Takeaway

Use BGREWRITEAOF to control AOF size, but monitor disk space and I/O to avoid rewrite failures.

screens.title: RDB vs AOF — tradeoffs and examplar use cases
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing RDB or AOF is a question of tradeoffs. RDB snapshots are compact and enable very fast restarts, which is useful for caches or situations where occasional recent write loss is acceptable. For example, a cache storing derived metrics that can be recomputed might prefer RDB only. AOF logs give better durability because they record every write. If your application requires minimal data loss — for instance a job queue where losing tasks is unacceptable — AOF with appendfsync everysec is the better choice. A combined approach is recommended for many critical deployments: RDB provides a compact fallback snapshot, while AOF offers near-real-time durability. If the AOF becomes corrupt, the RDB snapshot can still provide recovery. Misconceptions include thinking both always give strictly better results together: using both increases disk usage and operational complexity, so you must balance the benefit of redundancy against storage and restart cost. Evaluate your recovery time objectives, acceptable data-loss windows, and storage capacity to decide the right setup. RDB vs AOF — tradeoffs and examplar use cases means pick rdb for compact backups and fast restarts, aof for stronger durability; using both combines benefits but requires more disk and complexity.. In practical terms, when to use snapshots, logs, or both. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › RDB vs AOF
Comparison

Snapshots vs Journal

RDB
Compact binary snapshots; fast restarts; periodic data-loss window.
Use case
Caches and scenarios where some loss is acceptable.
AOF
Command journal offering finer durability depending on fsync policy.
Use case
Critical data like job queues where losing recent writes is costly.
RDB + AOF
Combine compact backups with near-real-time durability for most critical apps.
Tradeoff
Higher disk usage and complexity, but stronger recovery options.
Key Takeaway

Match persistence to how much recent write loss you can accept and how quickly you must restart.

Concrete scenarios
Caching only
RDB only is reasonable where cache warm-up is acceptable after restarts.
Critical data
AOF with appendfsync everysec reduces data loss to about one second, ideal for critical write data.
Most critical apps
Enable both RDB and AOF to get compact backups and replay-based durability as a combined strategy.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › redis.conf directives
Code Walkthrough

Essential persistence settings

These directives control how and where Redis writes RDB and AOF files.

# RDB: save if 1 write in 60 seconds
save 60 1

# AOF: enable and flush every second
appendonly yes
appendfilename "appendonly.aof"
appendfsync everysec

# AOF rewrite triggers
auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100
auto-aof-rewrite-min-size 64mb

# Persistence directory
dir /var/lib/redis
Explanation
save sets RDB snapshot conditions using time and change thresholds.
appendonly toggles AOF; appendfsync controls durability frequency.
dir must have correct permissions and enough disk space for temporary and final files.
Common mistake
Forgetting to free disk space in dir before starting persistence; running out of disk during a save can corrupt files.
Key Takeaway

Edit redis.conf carefully, restart Redis, and verify files exist in dir with proper permissions before relying on persistence.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Manual persistence
Commands

SAVE, BGSAVE, BGREWRITEAOF

Know which commands block and which run asynchronously, and why resource checks matter before running them.

SAVE
Synchronous RDB save that blocks the server — avoid in production.
BGSAVE
Asynchronous RDB save via a forked child; preferred for manual snapshots.
BGREWRITEAOF
Asynchronous AOF rewrite to compact the log and remove redundant commands.
Operational checklist
  • Check free disk space in the persistence dir before running BGSAVE or BGREWRITEAOF.
  • Monitor CPU and memory, since forking duplicates memory mappings temporarily.
  • Use BGSAVE for regular snapshots and BGREWRITEAOF for AOF compaction when necessary.
Concrete example
Run BGSAVE, wait for completion, then run BGREWRITEAOF to minimize AOF size after a burst of writes.
Key Takeaway

Prefer BGSAVE and BGREWRITEAOF for non-blocking operations; never run manual persistence without checking disk and resource headroom.

screens.title: Safety and operational best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Persistence operations interact closely with the operating system. You must ensure the persistence directory has sufficient disk space and correct permissions; otherwise a save or rewrite can fail or cause corruption. Back up RDB and AOF files to an external location regularly, ideally off-site, so hardware failures do not result in total data loss. Monitor disk input and output and server load during saves because the forked child and extra input and output can increase latency or C P U usage. Keep an eye on automatic rewrite activity and configure sensible thresholds for auto-aof-rewrite-percentage and min-size. A common operational mistake is enabling persistence and forgetting to verify that files are being written; after editing redis. conf restart Redis and confirm the RDB and AOF files appear in the dir. Finally, consider combining RDB and AOF for important datasets so that an AOF failure still leaves you a recent snapshot. Practically, schedule rewrites during off-peak hours if possible and set up alerts for low disk space and failed persistence operations. Safety and operational best practices means always verify disk space and permissions, back up persistence files off-site, and monitor rewrite activity and i/o during saves.. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Operational Best Practices
Checklist

Prepare for safe persistence

  • Ensure persistence directory has ample free disk space and correct user permissions.
  • Back up RDB and AOF files to an external location regularly.
  • Monitor disk I/O, CPU, and memory during BGSAVE and BGREWRITEAOF to detect load spikes.
  • Configure rewrite thresholds reasonably and schedule heavy operations during low traffic.
  • After editing redis.conf restart Redis and confirm expected files appear in the configured dir.
Common operational mistake
Not monitoring disk usage and letting the persistence directory fill up, which can interrupt saves and cause corruption.
Concrete actions
Set up alerts for free disk below a safe threshold.
Automate off-site backups of RDB and AOF files.
Review rewrite logs and monitor BGREWRITEAOF activity.
Key Takeaway

Operational safety is as important as the persistence mechanism; verify space/permissions and keep external backups and monitoring in place.

fullNarratorScript:
Redis is a memory-first database, which makes it very fast, but also means data in memory will be lost unless you persist it. In this lesson you will learn the two primary persistence mechanisms Redis provides: RDB snapshots, which capture point-in-time binary images of your dataset, and AOF logging, which records a journal of every write operation. You will see the tradeoffs: RDB is compact and excellent for fast restarts and backups but can lose recent writes between snapshots; AOF provides stronger durability by replaying commands but can grow larger and slow restarts. You will also learn the key redis. conf directives that control persistence, how to run manual saves safely using SAVE and BGSAVE, and practical scenarios where RDB only, AOF only, or a combined approach is appropriate. By the end, you will be able to choose a configuration that balances durability, performance, and operational safety for your application.

In this lesson you will build practical skills with Redis persistence. First, you will be able to distinguish RDB and AOF, explaining how each mechanism stores data and how they affect restart time and recovery guarantees. Second, you will learn how RDB snapshots are created and why Redis forks a child process to write the file, which keeps the server responsive during backups. Third, you will learn how AOF logs every write as a sequence of commands and how fsync choices control durability and performance. Finally, you will practice changing redis. conf settings and running manual commands like SAVE, BGSAVE, and BGREWRITEAOF. Each objective includes a small hands-on mental model so you can predict behavior during a crash and choose the right configuration for your application's tolerance for data loss. These skills will help you operate Redis with confidence and avoid common mistakes like running out of disk space during a save.

This page continues the objective list and focuses on hands-on operations and decision-making. You will learn to locate and edit redis. conf directives such as save, appendonly, appendfsync, appendfilename, and dir, and understand how each parameter influences persistence behavior. You will practice manual commands: SAVE for synchronous saves, BGSAVE for non-blocking snapshots, and BGREWRITEAOF to compact the append-only file. You will also learn to reason about when to keep both RDB and AOF enabled so you have a compact full backup and a near real-time journal, and how to recover if one file is corrupt. Finally, you will be trained to check disk space and permissions for the persistence directory to avoid the common pitfall of running out of space during a save operation. These objectives prepare you to configure and operate Redis persistence in production safely.

Persistence is the ability of Redis to store its in-memory dataset on disk so data survives restarts or crashes. Because Redis primarily serves and manipulates data in memory for speed, volatility is an inherent risk: if the process crashes or the host reboots, all volatile state disappears unless persisted. Practically, persistence turns an in-memory snapshot into a recoverable on-disk artifact. One concrete example: a session store using Redis without persistence could lose all active sessions after a restart, forcing users to reauthenticate. A common misconception is that persistence is only for databases that are not caches. In reality, many caching deployments also need persistence for warm restarts or graceful failover. Another misconception is that persistence eliminates every risk; it does not. Different persistence mechanisms trade off potential data loss windows, restart performance, and file size. The core decision is about acceptable data-loss tolerance. If your application can accept some recent writes being lost, RDB snapshots might be enough. If you require near-zero data loss, AOF with frequent fsync is preferable. Reflect: what data in your application cannot be recreated, and how much recent data loss would be tolerable?

RDB persistence creates point-in-time snapshots of the Redis dataset. The process begins when Redis decides to snapshot—either automatically via save directives or manually via SAVE/BGSAVE. Redis forks a child process; the child writes the entire dataset to a temporary RDB file on disk while the parent continues serving clients. When the child finishes writing and the file is safely on disk, Redis atomically replaces the old RDB with the new file. This fork-and-write approach offloads disk input and output to the child and keeps the main process responsive. A concrete example: a configuration like save 900 1 will create a snapshot if at least one write happens within 900 seconds. The main misconception to avoid is thinking RDB writes every change; it does not. It captures periodic full images, so any writes after the last snapshot but before a crash are lost. Advantages are compact binary files and fast restarts, making RDB excellent for backups and disaster recovery. Disadvantages are the data-loss window and the need for disk space to hold both temporary and final RDB files during writes. How RDB snapshots work means rdb uses a forked child to write a full binary snapshot to a temporary file then replaces the previous snapshot, balancing responsiveness and compact backups.. In practical terms, fork, write temporary file, and replace for compact backups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

AOF persistence records every write command Redis receives into an append-only log. Instead of saving full snapshots, AOF writes a sequence of redis commands that can be replayed at restart to reconstruct the dataset. This approach is like keeping a journal of changes: when Redis restarts it replays the logged commands in order to restore state. A key configuration is appendfsync, which controls when Redis calls fsync to flush buffered writes to physical disk. The common settings are always, everysec, and no. Using everysec is a practical compromise: it flushes the AOF roughly once per second, limiting potential data loss to about one second while keeping write latency low. A concrete example: enabling appendonly yes and appendfsync everysec causes every write to be appended immediately and the OS to be asked to flush the log at most once per second. Misconceptions include thinking AOF is always faster or smaller than RDB; in fact AOF files can be larger and restarts slower because commands must be replayed. AOF plus periodic rewrites gives strong durability with manageable file size growth. What is AOF (Append Only File) logging means aof logs all write commands for replay-based recovery; appendfsync controls durability versus performance tradeoffs.. In practical terms, a write-journal approach that records every write operation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

As writes accumulate, the append-only file grows because it stores every modifying command. To prevent unbounded growth and to remove redundant commands, Redis supports an automatic rewrite mechanism and the manual BGREWRITEAOF command. When rewriting, Redis creates a new optimized AOF by reading the current dataset and emitting a minimal set of commands that recreate it. This reduces file size and speeds up restarts. The auto-aof-rewrite-percentage and auto-aof-rewrite-min-size settings control when Redis triggers the rewrite; for example auto-aof-rewrite-percentage 100 means a rewrite runs when the AOF grows by 100% since the last rewrite. A common misunderstanding is that rewrites block the server. BGREWRITEAOF is asynchronous: it forks a child to create the new file, allowing the parent to continue serving clients. However, rewriting requires disk space for the temporary file and imposes extra input and output, so you must ensure sufficient disk capacity and monitor load. If a rewrite is interrupted or the disk fills, the AOF may remain large or become inconsistent, so keep backups and monitor rewrite activity. Choosing RDB or AOF is a question of tradeoffs. RDB snapshots are compact and enable very fast restarts, which is useful for caches or situations where occasional recent write loss is acceptable. For example, a cache storing derived metrics that can be recomputed might prefer RDB only. AOF logs give better durability because they record every write. If your application requires minimal data loss — for instance a job queue where losing tasks is unacceptable — AOF with appendfsync everysec is the better choice. A combined approach is recommended for many critical deployments: RDB provides a compact fallback snapshot, while AOF offers near-real-time durability. If the AOF becomes corrupt, the RDB snapshot can still provide recovery. Misconceptions include thinking both always give strictly better results together: using both increases disk usage and operational complexity, so you must balance the benefit of redundancy against storage and restart cost. Evaluate your recovery time objectives, acceptable data-loss windows, and storage capacity to decide the right setup.
